issues.explanation: For a 62-year-old male torture survivor, 'being looked at sexually' is difficult to reconcile with the rest of the profile. The other triggers, memories, appraisals, and strategies all point to persecution/institutional betrayal and disorientation rather than sexualized threat. Without any corresponding sexualized memory, threat, or appraisal content, this trigger stands out as clinically incoherent with the stated trauma pattern.

vignette: Eduardo had come to believe that the walls of the detention facility still pressed against his chest whenever the radio in the break room crackled to life. Years earlier, during a period of political purges in his home country, he had been taken from his apartment by men in dark uniforms. He remembered the heavy boots on the concrete stairs, the sterile scent of antiseptic, and the cracked television mounted in the corner of his cell, broadcasting news that justified his disappearance. When they brought him into the interrogation room, the guards spoke in a rapid, unfamiliar cadence, their voices overlapping into a wall of incomprehensible chatter that vibrated through the floor. Some hours were carved into his mind with impossible precision-the weight of the iron chair, the sharp smell of cordite, the taste of copper when they struck him-while entire days simply vanished, leaving him with no sense of what happened between one flash and the next. He watched the news screen even as the questioning began, certain that the state would erase him if he stopped looking at it, even though the broadcasts only confirmed that no one outside the walls knew he was there. When he was eventually released and resettled in this country, the quiet of his apartment felt heavier than the cell ever had. He stopped going out on weekends, then on weekdays, until the habit of staying indoors became his default rhythm. He began rehearsing every exchange before it happened, standing in front of his bathroom mirror and shaping his sentences until his jaw ached, worried that an unscripted pause might make him look vulnerable. The memories arrived as sudden, total invasions: the smell of damp wool, the taste of dust, the feel of a hand on his shoulder, all pressing in at once as if the room were collapsing inward. He steered his mind toward mundane calculations-counting ceiling tiles, reciting pharmacology dosages-anything that would pull his thoughts toward something else. He lives alone, and the silence of his evenings has stretched into years, mirroring the quiet distance that grew between him and the cultural circles he once knew. Now, as a psychiatrist in a bustling urban clinic, the old patterns dictate his days. He works in a wing where security guards wear navy uniforms, and he keeps his office door closed, watching the hallway from the periphery. In the staff lounge, a television mounted above the coffee machine plays news segments about foreign conflicts, and Eduardo feels his throat tighten the moment the screen lights up, prompting him to step out before the volume grows. The clinic's waiting area fills with people speaking a dozen dialects, and the overlapping voices sometimes make him freeze at his desk, his pen hovering over a chart. He no longer attends neighborhood festivals or visits the markets where he once bought coffee with neighbors who shared his language; the familiar feels distant, and he accepts that the men who held him in that room are gone or hiding, that no trial will ever bring accountability, and that the institutions that should have intervened simply turned away. Eduardo finally walked into the intake office because he caught himself rehearsing a conversation with a colleague for twenty minutes before stepping into a meeting, and he realized he could no longer tell where the script ended and his own thoughts began. He sits across from me now, hands folded, waiting to see if this space will feel like a cell disguised as a clinic. What he most hopes for is a way to hear the news without his pulse spiking, to walk through the city without calculating his route, to let a conversation unfold without a prepared line. What he fears, more than anything, is that the boundaries he spent decades drawing will become permanent, and that the community he left behind will remain out of reach, forever just beyond the sound of a language he no longer recognizes himself speaking.
